claim: A contact-model-agnostic task-space framework achieves accurate 6-DoF compliant motion and 6-D wrench regulation on position-controlled arms; practical admittance improves coupled stability while ideal time-varying impedance can lose passivity and oscillate under constraint, and human ultrasound demonstrations remain qualitative.
problem_and_setting: General compliant motion and multidimensional contact-wrench regulation for position-controlled robot arms in constrained scanning interactions, without an explicit tissue constitutive model.
method_or_mechanism: Ideal, practical, and hybrid task-space admittance controllers are derived. The ideal controller favors free-space tracking; the practical controller uses measured feedback and instantaneous rendered impedance for better constrained stability at some tracking cost; the hybrid combines the behaviors. Gravity and inertia compensation are included.
content_summary: Mean compliant-trajectory error is below 0.30 mm. Five-trial phantom tests at 3 N report mean relative force error below 0.5% and maximum below 3% after convergence, with and without lateral scan motion. Five-trial 6-D tests at 3 N and 0.2 Nm report mean errors below 0.5% force and 0.8% moment, maxima below 2.2%. Analysis and an operator-constraint experiment show ideal time-varying impedance can oscillate, while practical feedback improves stability. Human kidney, spine, and carotid 3-D ultrasound demonstrations are qualitative.
synthesis_role: Strong contact-model-agnostic baseline and direct evidence that variable gains must be judged through rendered passivity and coupled stability, not nominal impedance alone.
development_link: A richer contact model must show incremental failure-inclusive benefit beyond nominal force accuracy: transient overshoot, safety limits, stability under time-varying gains, heterogeneity and relaxation, held-out anatomy, finite-area wrench, or quantitative image outcomes.

evidence.finding: Ideal, practical, and hybrid task-space admittance control provides 6-DoF compliant motion and 6-D wrench regulation on position-controlled arms.
Ideal time-varying impedance can fail passivity and coupled stability; practical feedback improves constrained stability at a free-space tracking cost.
The ideal controller oscillates when an operator constrains the robot.
Mean compliant-trajectory error is below 0.30 mm.
Across five trials with and without lateral scanning, mean relative force error is below 0.5% and maximum post-convergence error below 3%.
Across five trials at 3 N and 0.2 Nm, mean relative errors are below 0.5% for force and 0.8% for moment, with maxima below 2.2%.
Kidney, spine, and carotid 3-D ultrasound are demonstrated but only qualitatively because prior non-rigid target geometry is unavailable.

boundary_conditions: Practical stability trades against free-space accuracy
Commanded time-varying impedance need not be passively rendered
assumptions: Measured task-space feedback suffices without tissue identification
Gravity and inertia compensation are adequate
Rendered impedance is meaningful for stability assessment
Phantom trials inform accuracy but not in-vivo generalization

reported: Ideal time-varying impedance can lose passivity and stability
Practical control trades free-space accuracy for stability
Human results lack quantitative geometry validation
inferred: Post-convergence force error does not bound impact, pressure, deformation, or dose
Explicit contact identification is not shown necessary for nominal tracking
No quantitative in-vivo clinical benefit is established
Richer models are unjustified unless they improve transient safety, stability, image quality, or held-out heterogeneity

conflicts_with: Explicit tissue modeling is required for sub-percent mean phantom force regulation
Nominal tracking accuracy proves passivity or coupled stability
Safety under impact, heterogeneity, or relaxation
